> when at fifty years of age and ewura was dismissed from her job she gracefully moved into her own dream house her colleagues were stunned had she stolen from the official coffers they whispered among themselves but they knew too well that ewura had been only an ordinary classroom teacher in a roman catholic school and she therefore had no means of controlling any official monies her background was simply this ewura had learnt from childhood that nothing was more essential to ones well-being than shelter she had as far back as those early childhood days determined that when she grew up the first thing she would do could be to buy herself a house when the socialist policies of ghana brought hire purchase within the reach of the working classes ewura saw and heard an opportunity knock at her door she grabbed it she scrapped and pinched from several part time jobs saved every penny she could for the required deposit and collected the keys to the estate before she turned twenty seven
answer:
> [!answer]
> When, at fifty years of age, Ewura was dismissed from her job, she gracefully moved into her own dream house. Her colleagues were stunned. "Had she stolen from the official coffers?" they whispered among themselves. But they knew too well that Ewura had been only an ordinary classroom teacher in a Roman Catholic school, and she therefore had no means of controlling any official monies. Her background was simply this: Ewura had learnt from childhood that nothing was more essential to one's well-being than shelter. She had, as far back as those early childhood days, determined that when she grew up, the first thing she would do would be to buy herself a house. When the socialist policies of Ghana brought hire purchase within the reach of the working classes, Ewura saw and heard an opportunity knock at her door. She grabbed it. She scrimped and pinched from several part-time jobs, saved every penny she could for the required deposit, and collected the keys to the estate before she turned twenty-seven.
>
> _Key points:_ capitals for **sentence beginnings** and **proper nouns** (Ewura, Roman Catholic, Ghana); **commas** around the parenthetical _at fifty years of age_ and _as far back as those early childhood days_; a **question mark** and **quotation marks** for the colleagues' question; a **colon** before the explanation (_simply this:_); the **apostrophe** in _one's_; **hyphens** in _part-time_ and _twenty-seven_; **commas in the series** _scrimped…, saved…, and collected…_. body:
The passage below contains some **concord errors**. Identify and correct them.

> The nations in the western world where class struggle were often sublimated by high wages and decent social welfare provision maintains a relatively stable system only because of historic shifts away from unfettered capitalism. But such social institutions is aberrations, the result of class struggle or a historic alignment of political and economic factors. Either way, the underlying accumulation of capital always reassert the primacy of capitalist decline in the end. Before we discuss the notions of capitalism, including the laws and tendencies, there are also trends and cycles which exposes the rhythm capitalist profits to be discussed. Because of the internal dynamics of capitalism, there is an inherent tendency towards breakdown – this is known as the business cycle or boom and bust as some people like to call it. So what is something specific about how crisis develop under capitalism and how they disrupts the apparent equilibrium of the system? A passage in the Communist Manifesto indicate the beginnings of Marx's theory of capitalist crisis. He writes, “In these crises, …. Society suddenly finds itself put back into a state of momentary barbarism; it appears as if a famine, a universal war of devastation, had cut off the supply of every means of subsistence; industry and commerce seems to be destroyed; and why? Marx explain that it is because there is “too much civilization, too much means of subsistence, too much industry, too much commerce.”
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _class struggle **were**_ → **class struggle was** (singular subject).
> 2. _The nations … **maintains**_ → **The nations … maintain** (plural head noun _nations_).
> 3. _such social institutions **is** aberrations_ → **such social institutions are aberrations**.
> 4. _the underlying accumulation of capital always **reassert**_ → **always reasserts** (head noun _accumulation_ is singular).
> 5. _trends and cycles which **exposes**_ → **which expose** (the relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent _trends and cycles_).
> 6. _how crisis **develop**_ → **how crises develop** (plural to agree with _they_ that follows; or _how a crisis develops_).
> 7. _how they **disrupts**_ → **how they disrupt**.
> 8. _A passage … **indicate**_ → **A passage … indicates**.
> 9. _industry and commerce **seems**_ → **industry and commerce seem** (compound subject joined by _and_).
> 10. _Marx **explain**_ → **Marx explains**.
>
> _(Quoted words from Marx are left as in the source.)_
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Concord (subject–verb agreement)**: the verb agrees with the **head** of the subject, not with nouns in modifying phrases (_The nations in the western world … maintain_); **relative pronouns** take the number of their antecedent; **compound subjects** joined by _and_ are plural; singular proper names take singular verbs.

## Simplified explanation

Match each verb to its real subject: **nations maintain**, **institutions are**, **accumulation reasserts**, **trends expose**, **crises develop**, **they disrupt**, **a passage indicates**, **industry and commerce seem**, **Marx explains**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject, then check its verb.

body:
Read the following passage and **analyse the sentences into their structural types** (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex).

> (1) John is not going to university because of the following reasons. (2) In the first place, his family is quite poor and since he has four young brothers and sisters still at school, he feels he should help his family financially as soon as possible. (3) Also, due to the poor state of the family, utility bills such as water and electricity are not paid. (4) The family also cannot afford three-square meal per day. (5) Secondly, if he went to university, his mother would be left alone to look after the young children. (6) This problem can make her life develop high blood pressure. (7) Apart from this, the children can become recalcitrant as a result of lack of good parental care. (8) Finally, he has been offered a good job with excellent chances of promotion. (9) With his monthly income, John will earn enough money and he will support his family financially and also save some money for his education. (10) John wants to go to the university but he is going to take the job instead.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | No. | Type | Reason |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 | **Simple** | One main clause; _because of the following reasons_ is a phrase. |
> | 2 | **Compound-complex** | Two main clauses (_his family is quite poor_ / _he feels…_) joined by _and_, plus subordinate clauses (_since he has…_, _(that) he should help…_). |
> | 3 | **Simple** | One clause; _due to the poor state…_ and _such as…_ are phrases. |
> | 4 | **Simple** | One clause. |
> | 5 | **Complex** | Main clause _his mother would be left alone…_ + adverbial clause _if he went to university_. |
> | 6 | **Simple** | One clause (_to develop_/_develop high blood pressure_ is a non-finite complement). |
> | 7 | **Simple** | One clause with phrases. |
> | 8 | **Simple** | One clause. |
> | 9 | **Compound** | Two main clauses joined by _and_: _John will earn…_ / _he will support… and also save…_. |
> | 10 | **Compound** | Two main clauses joined by _but_. |
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Simple:** one independent clause. **Compound:** two or more independent clauses joined by coordinators (_and, but, or_) or a semicolon. **Complex:** one independent clause + at least one dependent clause (introduced by subordinators: _because, since, if, that, who_). **Compound-complex:** two or more independent clauses + at least one dependent clause. Phrases (_because of…_, _due to…_) do not make clauses.

## Simplified explanation

Count the clauses: one = **simple**; two joined by _and/but_ = **compound**; one main + an _if/since/that_ clause = **complex**; both = **compound-complex**.
hint: Count finite clauses and check the linking words.

body:
Read the following passage carefully and write a **summary** of it in **90–120 words**.

> Eggs are in different types. Fertile eggs can be incubated and developed into chicks. Like other eggs, they are [equally] nutritious and have equal cholesterol content. Fertile eggs have no special advantages over other eggs. However, they have two significant disadvantages. First, they do not keep as well as unfertilized eggs, and second, they cost more. Organic eggs are produced by hens fed with 'organic' feeds (i.e. grains grown without pesticides or commercial fertilizers) and raised without medications. Organic eggs have the same nutrient content as other eggs, but they are more expensive because of their higher production cost. Again, true free range eggs are produced by hens raised outdoors or with daily access to the outdoors. … Free-range production does not affect the nutritional value or cholesterol level of eggs; it does increase the price, however.
>
> The attraction in eggs lies in the color of the shell. Mostly, the breed of the hen determines the color of the egg's shell. … Shell has nothing to do with quality, flavor or nutritional value. The price of brown eggs is usually a bit higher … because the brown-shell producing breeds [are] birds with bigger appetites for feed.
>
> Apart from attraction, eggs are highly nutritious. One large egg provides about six grams of protein … Egg white is considered an ideal protein … Eggs are a significant source of iron, riboflavin, folate and vitamins B12, D, and E. … The only nutrient not found in an egg is vitamin C.
>
> Eggs have other desirable properties in addition to their nutritional value. They are inexpensive, convenient, easy to prepare and easy to chew. … Eggs also play important roles in a wide variety of recipes …
>
> To protect themselves against bacteria in eggs, consumers should not eat raw eggs or food that contain raw eggs. Dirty, cracked or outdated eggs should never be bought. Also, eggs must be cooked well … eggs should be stored in the refrigerator … Lastly, everything must be kept clean while handling, preparing and serving the food.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (about 110 words):**
>
> Eggs come in several types. Fertile, organic and free-range eggs have the same nutritional value and cholesterol as ordinary eggs but cost more; fertile eggs also keep less well. Shell colour, which depends on the hen's breed, attracts buyers but does not affect quality, flavour or nutrition, although brown eggs cost slightly more. Eggs are highly nutritious, supplying high-quality protein, mostly unsaturated fat, iron, riboflavin, folate and vitamins B12, D and E; only vitamin C is absent. They are also cheap, convenient, easy to prepare and chew, and useful in many recipes. To avoid bacteria, consumers should not eat raw eggs, should buy only clean, uncracked, fresh eggs, cook them well, refrigerate them and keep everything clean.
>
> _Outline alternative:_ (1) Types of eggs and their cost; (2) shell colour; (3) nutritional value; (4) other advantages; (5) safety measures.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A good summary **captures the main idea of each paragraph**, omits **examples, illustrations, repetitions and figures**, uses **your own words** and **continuous prose**, stays within the **word limit**, and adds no personal comment. Topic sentences (often the first sentence of each paragraph) guide selection.

## Simplified explanation

Write one point for each paragraph: **types (same nutrition, higher cost)**, **shell colour (no effect)**, **nutrients**, **other benefits**, **safety tips**, in about 100 words.
hint: One sentence per paragraph's main idea; drop examples and figures.

body:
Study the passage below and either write an **outline** of it or **summarise** it in **100 words**.

> The vulture is seen differently from other birds that have the temerity to scavenge for their 'livelihood'. This is because of its business of rummaging through refuse dumpsites and doing justice to dead 'material'. Even though most of our folktales present the good side of this bird, the vulture does more for us than the folktales present.
>
> Vultures are magnificent birds that have huge environmental and economic importance. Vultures are specially designed to dispose of animal and human waste and to prevent the spread of diseases. Nature has equipped vultures with a digestive system that contains special acids that dissolve anthrax, botulism, rabies and cholera bacteria. By consuming the carcasses of diseased animals, vultures prevent the spread of these life-threatening diseases.
>
> Vultures face tremendous challenges all over the world for survival. Each year, a day is marked as International Vulture Awareness Day … There are 23 species of vulture the world over. Currently, there is a decline of 42 percent of vulture numbers … in the past 30 years, with Rüppell's Vulture declining by a whopping 85 percent. The birds face serious threats like hatred, persecution, poisoning, vehicular collision, electrocution, starvation and destruction of their breeding sites.
>
> … In order to reduce the rate of extinction of vultures, there should be appropriate legislation and other control measures to prevent the indiscriminate use of poison … Advocates are also calling for support for captive breeding programmes and other conservation initiatives … Captive breeding centres have been set up in Pakistan, India and Nepal … The ramifications of a world without vultures will mean that there will be an increase in feral dogs, consequently putting all of us at risk of rabies attacks and possible deaths.
>
> Experts see vultures as 'unsung environmental heroes' and believe that a world without vultures would be a foul-smelling place filled with diseases and rotten carcasses. … We all need to save vultures from becoming extinct in the environment to safeguard biodiversity.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (about 100 words):**
>
> Although vultures are despised as scavengers, they benefit people more than folktales suggest. Their powerful digestive acids destroy the bacteria of anthrax, botulism, rabies and cholera, so by eating waste and diseased carcasses they prevent the spread of deadly diseases. However, vultures are declining sharply worldwide because of hatred, persecution, poisoning, road collisions, electrocution, starvation and loss of breeding sites. To prevent their extinction, governments should pass laws against indiscriminate poisoning and support captive breeding and other conservation programmes. Without vultures, feral dogs, rabies and other diseases would increase, so these environmental heroes must be protected to safeguard biodiversity.
>
> **Outline alternative:**
> 1. Introduction: vultures are undervalued scavengers.
> 2. Importance: waste disposal and disease prevention.
> 3. Threats: a steep decline from human activities.
> 4. Remedies: legislation, captive breeding, conservation.
> 5. Conclusion: a world without vultures would be diseased; save them.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In an **outline**, main points are numbered and sub-points indented, using parallel phrases; in a **summary**, main ideas are linked in coherent prose. Both exclude illustrative details (23 species, 42%, India's vulture restaurant).

## Simplified explanation

Say: vultures are **useful (they prevent disease)**, are **disappearing because of humans**, need **laws and breeding programmes**, and **must be saved**, all in about 100 words.
hint: Main idea per paragraph: value, threats, remedies, consequences.

body:
Read the following passage carefully and write an **outline or summary** of it (**90–120 words**).

> Governments argue that taxes are a necessary evil – the price we pay in a civilized society. Whether you agree with that sentiment or not, it is undeniable that the price is usually a high one. Taxes can be divided into two categories: direct and indirect. Income tax, corporate tax and property tax are examples of direct tax. Of these, income tax is probably the most resented. This is especially so in countries where income tax is progressive – the more you earn, the more you pay. Critics have an aversion for progressive taxes, for as they usually assert, these taxes are used as punitive and oppressive measures particularly aimed at those who have worked hard to build up their business.
>
> Indirect taxes include sales tax, taxes on liquor and cigarettes, and customs duties. These are less visible than direct taxes but can still deal an economic blow, especially among the poor. … Regrettably, workers … have a huge chunk of their income consumed by ever-mounting taxes. High taxes on items of mass consumption, such as soap and liquor, evidently create this unfortunate situation.
>
> The question is what do governments do with all the money they collect? The provision of basic and essential public utilities, such as facilities for schools and equipment for hospitals and infrastructure, take vast sums of money … Taxes are needed to pay [public workers'] salaries. … they may be used for the provision of social amenities … Taxes have also been used to ensure a congenial atmosphere for healthy living. … western European countries have introduced environmental tax mostly as a means of reducing air pollution. In some areas, progressive taxes are used to bridge the gap between the rich and the poor.
>
> It has also been noted that in South Africa, for instance, taxes make up about 51% of the cost of alcohol and cigarettes to curb drinking and smoking. … Thus taxes may serve as a tool to encourage or discourage certain forms of behaviour. Indeed, few people will acknowledge the benefits that taxes bring to their communities, but nobody would seriously argue that we will be better off without them.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (about 105 words):**
>
> Taxes, which governments describe as a necessary evil, are usually burdensome. They are either direct, such as income, corporate and property taxes, or indirect, such as sales taxes, excise duties on alcohol and cigarettes, and customs duties. Progressive income tax is particularly resented as punishing hard work, while indirect taxes on everyday goods hit the poor hardest. Nevertheless, tax revenue pays for schools, hospitals, infrastructure, social amenities and public workers' salaries. Taxes are also used to reduce pollution, narrow the gap between rich and poor, and discourage harmful behaviour such as drinking and smoking. Although people rarely acknowledge their benefits, society cannot do without taxes.
>
> **Outline alternative:**
> 1. Taxes: a necessary but heavy burden.
> 2. Types: direct (resented progressive income tax) and indirect (burden on the poor).
> 3. Uses: public services, salaries, amenities.
> 4. Other functions: environment, equality, behaviour control.
> 5. Conclusion: taxes are indispensable.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Summary technique: identify **topic sentences**, delete **examples** (South Africa's 51%, one worker in four), **generalise** lists (schools, hospitals, roads → public services), and **combine** related points with linking words (_nevertheless, also, although_).

## Simplified explanation

Taxes are **heavy** (direct and indirect, hurting workers and the poor) but **fund services and salaries**, **protect the environment**, **reduce inequality** and **discourage smoking and drinking**, so we **need them**.
hint: Types, burden, uses, other functions, conclusion.

body:
**Punctuate** the following passage.

> With hands clasped in supplication a one-year-old girl strapped to her back and another sitting on a piece of brown cloth spread on the ground she chants in a boring monotone please brother give alms for the twins shes been doing this at the bustling Tema bus station everyday for the past six months. But Auntie Mansa refuses to admit she is a beggar. She believes she is just doing what tradition requires. She says when I delivered my first set of twins the oracle revealed that the babies were dancers who required to be carried to the market-place to dance everyday and collect alms. She ignored the instruction and about two months later the twins died one after the other within a week. So when she was blessed with the present set she paid heed immediately Auntie Mansa is not alone in this trade. She and those of her kind can easily be distinguished from the handicapped who take begging as a profession. What do other members of the republic think about it Mr Ibu is worried these people he says exploit Gods gift to enrich themselves
answer:
> [!answer]
> With hands clasped in supplication, a one-year-old girl strapped to her back and another sitting on a piece of brown cloth spread on the ground, she chants in a boring monotone, "Please, brother, give alms for the twins." She's been doing this at the bustling Tema bus station every day for the past six months. But Auntie Mansa refuses to admit she is a beggar. She believes she is just doing what tradition requires. She says, "When I delivered my first set of twins, the oracle revealed that the babies were dancers who required to be carried to the market-place to dance every day and collect alms." She ignored the instruction and, about two months later, the twins died one after the other within a week. So, when she was blessed with the present set, she paid heed immediately. Auntie Mansa is not alone in this trade. She and those of her kind can easily be distinguished from the handicapped who take begging as a profession. What do other members of the republic think about it? Mr Ibu is worried. "These people," he says, "exploit God's gift to enrich themselves."
>
> _Key points:_ the long introductory phrase (_With hands clasped… on the ground_) ends with a **comma** before the main clause _she chants_; **direct speech** gets a comma before it, **quotation marks** and a capital; the vocative _brother_ is set off by commas; **apostrophes** in _She's_ and _God's_; **question mark** after _about it_; the interrupted quotation _"These people," he says, "exploit…"_. (_Everyday_ as an adverb should be **every day**.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Rules: commas after long introductory phrases and clauses; commas around vocatives (_Please, brother, …_); quotation marks for direct speech with a comma introducing it; apostrophes for contractions and possession; question marks for direct questions; split quotations with commas on both sides of the reporting clause.

## Simplified explanation

Add **commas** after the long opening phrase, **quotation marks** around what she and Mr Ibu say, **apostrophes** (_She's_, _God's_) and a **question mark**.
hint: Look for direct speech, possessives and the long opening phrase.

body:
**Punctuate** the following passage.

> Mr Schandorfs attitude to life should be emulated by everybody in 2010 he invested fifty thousand cedis in citrus punch company two years later the companys shares started depreciating. However Mr Thompson who stayed on with the company lost all his investment because the company eventually went totally bankrupt it is worth noting that while in the university Mr Schandorf had remarked I believe in the philosophy of acting promptly and striking elsewhere. Mr Schandorf had also read a book entitled never despair in life which really changed his thinking. The lesson to learn is this when we lose out on some venture that should not spell doom for us
answer:
> [!answer]
> Mr Schandorf's attitude to life should be emulated by everybody. In 2010, he invested fifty thousand cedis in Citrus Punch Company. Two years later, the company's shares started depreciating. However, Mr Thompson, who stayed on with the company, lost all his investment because the company eventually went totally bankrupt. It is worth noting that, while in the university, Mr Schandorf had remarked, "I believe in the philosophy of acting promptly and striking elsewhere." Mr Schandorf had also read a book entitled _Never Despair in Life_, which really changed his thinking. The lesson to learn is this: when we lose out on some venture, that should not spell doom for us.
>
> _Key points:_ **sentence boundaries** (_everybody. In 2010_; _depreciating._; _bankrupt. It_); **apostrophes** (_Schandorf's_, _company's_); **capitals** for the company's name and the book title; **commas** after _In 2010_, _Two years later_ and _However_; the **non-restrictive clause** _who stayed on with the company_ between commas; **direct speech** with a comma and quotation marks; the book title in **italics** (or underlined in handwriting); a **colon** before the explanation; a comma after the introductory clause _when we lose out on some venture_.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Common errors in this passage are run-on sentences (fused sentences), missing apostrophes of possession, and failure to mark titles and direct speech. A colon introduces an explanation or elaboration of what precedes (_this:_).

## Simplified explanation

Split it into sentences, add **apostrophes** (_Schandorf's_, _company's_), **commas**, **quotation marks** for his remark, **capitalise/italicise** the book title, and use a **colon** after _this_.
hint: Find where each sentence ends first.

body:
Rewrite the following passage and **restore all the punctuation marks** appropriately.

> many of our youth run away from hardships at home only to meet unbearable conditions abroad the youth as future leaders must be properly trained in readiness for life without any working experience how can they run the affairs of the country in future greater emphasis should be laid on vocational and technical training to enable the youth to be self employed these were the words of the sector minister at a public lecture the countrys economy must meet the true needs of young people for their survival and integration into society in his book seeking greener pastures bob james postulated that many teenage youth had been lured into foreign countries for better life but which becomes bitter on arrival at their final destinations despite the fact that many of our youth have returned to tell their horrible stories others still venture overseas unfortunately those who lure them give lurid stories of how honey flows in these european and asian countries and which can transform their lives overnight
answer:
> [!answer]
> Many of our youth run away from hardships at home, only to meet unbearable conditions abroad. "The youth, as future leaders, must be properly trained in readiness for life. Without any working experience, how can they run the affairs of the country in future? Greater emphasis should be laid on vocational and technical training to enable the youth to be self-employed." These were the words of the sector Minister at a public lecture. "The country's economy must meet the true needs of young people for their survival and integration into society." In his book, _Seeking Greener Pastures_, Bob James postulated that many teenage youth had been lured into foreign countries for a better life, which becomes bitter on arrival at their final destinations. Despite the fact that many of our youth have returned to tell their horrible stories, others still venture overseas. Unfortunately, those who lure them give lurid stories of how honey flows in these European and Asian countries, which can transform their lives overnight.
>
> _Key points:_ capitals (sentence openings, _Bob James_, _European_, _Asian_, _Minister_); the **question mark** after _in future_; **quotation marks** for the Minister's words; **hyphen** in _self-employed_; **apostrophe** in _country's_; the **book title** in italics; commas after introductory elements (_Without any working experience_, _Despite the fact…_, _Unfortunately_) and around the parenthetical _as future leaders_. (_but which_ and _and which_ are faulty constructions; the relative clause should follow directly.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Restoring punctuation requires identifying **sentence boundaries**, **direct speech** (the Minister's words), **titles**, **proper adjectives** (European, Asian), **compound words** (self-employed), and **possessives**.

## Simplified explanation

Break into sentences, add a **question mark**, **quotation marks** for the Minister, the **hyphen** in _self-employed_, the **apostrophe** in _country's_, and **capitalise** names and the book title.
hint: Mark the question, the quoted speech, the title and possessives.

body:
The passage below contains **subject–verb agreement errors**. Identify and correct them. (Do not copy the passage.)

> The spate of road accidents in Ghana continues to dominate discussions in the country … especially, as statistics on road accidents over the year has consistently featured the highest office of the country, the presidency. Interestingly, the safety of the presidential convoy in Ghana have been threatened on several occasions not by terrorist attacks but by fatal road accidents that have claimed the lives of security personnel, journalists and presidential staffers who usually travels around the country with the President. The persistent involvement of the presidential convoy in road accidents and the cost to the nation calls for a review of the security of the President from a safety perspective. The dossier about presidential accidents in Ghana show that every President in the Fourth Republic have been involved in some fatal accident of some sort. The first and notable characteristic of the nature of travel of the President are the speed at which the convoy moves. There is indeed studies and instances that support the need for presidential convoy to move at such speeds … The high risk of exposure of the Presidential convoy to road accidents due to the speed at which the convoy [moves] reveal that the security of the President including the security personnel are not as threatened as the safety of the President and his entourage. But eliminating all other factors including time, by ensuring the presidential convoy take into consideration the time of departure and arrival …, the issue of security remain prominent on the list of excuses … A more appropriate solution may be to move at reasonable speed limits that allows drivers … enough time to avert any likely accidents.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _statistics on road accidents … **has**_ → **statistics … have** (plural).
> 2. _the safety of the presidential convoy … **have** been threatened_ → **the safety … has been threatened** (head noun _safety_).
> 3. _staffers who usually **travels**_ → **staffers who usually travel** (_who_ refers to the plural _personnel, journalists and staffers_).
> 4. _The persistent involvement … and the cost … **calls**_ → **call** (compound subject joined by _and_).
> 5. _The dossier … **show**_ → **The dossier … shows**.
> 6. _every President … **have** been involved_ → **every President … has been involved** (_every_ + singular).
> 7. _The first and notable characteristic … **are** the speed_ → **is** (one characteristic).
> 8. _There **is** indeed studies and instances_ → **There are** (the real subject _studies and instances_ is plural).
> 9. _The high risk of exposure … **reveal**_ → **reveals** (head noun _risk_).
> 10. _the security of the President including the security personnel **are**_ → **is** (head noun _security_; _including…_ is parenthetical).
> 11. _the presidential convoy **take**_ → **takes**.
> 12. _the issue of security **remain**_ → **remains**.
>
> (_continues_ and _that allows_ (agreeing with _a more appropriate solution_) are already correct; strictly _limits that allow_ if _limits_ is taken as the antecedent.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Key concord rules illustrated: the **head noun** governs (not nouns in _of_-phrases); **compound subjects** with _and_ take plural verbs; **every/each** + singular; in **existential 'there'** sentences the verb agrees with the notional subject that follows; **relative pronouns** take the number of their antecedents; parenthetical phrases (_including, together with, as well as_) do not change the number.

## Simplified explanation

Match each verb to its true subject: **statistics have**, **safety has**, **staffers travel**, **involvement and cost call**, **dossier shows**, **every President has**, **characteristic is**, **there are studies**, **risk reveals**, **security is**, **convoy takes**, **issue remains**.
hint: For each verb, find the head noun of its subject.

body:
Read the passage below and (a) **identify the subject–verb agreement errors**, (b) **correct them**. Do not copy the entire passage.

> There are lots of facts to know about fungi. A plant without leaves, flowers or green colouring matter and which grow on other plants or decaying materials are called fungus. The cells of fungi are very small and possesses discrete membrane-bound nuclei. The concern of this discourse are to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of fungi to living organisms. A number of research has found some disadvantages of fungi. Fungi are disadvantageous to man because they destroy food, causes foot-rot, produce ringworm, damages industrial equipment and pollutes water. However, fungi are useful in fertilizing the soil and serving as source of food. Available statistics in most countries indicates that soil fungi make up 10 to 30 percent of soil rhizosphere. Furthermore, other advantages of fungi includes their industrial use for baking and brewing medicine and for the manufacture of organic substances.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _A plant … which **grow**_ → **which grows** (antecedent _a plant_ is singular).
> 2. _A plant … **are** called fungus_ → **is called a fungus**.
> 3. _The cells of fungi … **possesses**_ → **possess**.
> 4. _The concern of this discourse **are**_ → **is**.
> 5. _A number of research **has** found_ → the phrase is faulty because _research_ is uncountable: **A number of studies have found** (or _Research has found_).
> 6. _they destroy food, **causes** foot-rot … **damages** … **pollutes**_ → **cause … damage … pollute** (the subject _they_ is plural).
> 7. _Available statistics … **indicates**_ → **indicate**.
> 8. _other advantages of fungi **includes**_ → **include**.
>
> (_There are lots of facts_, _fungi are disadvantageous_, _they destroy… produce_, _fungi make up_ are correct.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Notes: **a number of** + plural noun + plural verb (vs **the number of** + singular verb); uncountable nouns (_research, information, advice_) cannot follow _a number of_; every verb in a **series** sharing the same subject must agree with it.

## Simplified explanation

Fix: **which grows**, **is called**, **possess**, **concern is**, **studies have**, **cause/damage/pollute**, **statistics indicate**, **advantages include**.
hint: Watch the verbs in lists and in relative clauses.

body:
The sentences in the passage below have been numbered. Indicate the **structural type** of each sentence.

> (1) The dress and its arrangement upon the person is generally found to be the index of the man or woman. (2) In dress, it is our privilege to honour our creator. (3) Because we are to be representative of Him, our appearance in every respect should be characterized by neatness, modesty and purity. (4) Since we judge of a person's character by the style of dress worn, a modest, godly person will dress modestly, and a refined taste, a cultivated mind will be revealed in the choice of simple, appropriate attire. (5) We should seek to make the best of our appearance. (6) The one who is simple and unpretending in her dress and in her manners shows that she understands that the true person is characterized by moral simplicity. (7) If the world introduces a modest, convenient, and healthful mode of dress, it will not change our relationship with God. (8) Do not occupy your time by endeavoring to follow all the foolish fashions in dress. (9) Dress neatly and becomingly, but do not make yourself the subject of remarks either by being over-dressed or by dressing in lax, untidy manner. (10) Act as though you knew that the eyes of heaven is upon you, and you are living under the approbation or disapprobation of God.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | No. | Type | Reason |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 | **Simple** | One finite clause (_is generally found_). |
> | 2 | **Simple** | One clause (the infinitive _to honour_ is non-finite). |
> | 3 | **Complex** | Adverbial clause _Because we are…_ + main clause. |
> | 4 | **Compound-complex** | Two main clauses joined by _and_ (_a modest person will dress modestly_ / _a refined taste… will be revealed_) + the subordinate clause _Since we judge…_. |
> | 5 | **Simple** | One clause. |
> | 6 | **Complex** | Main clause _The one… shows_ + relative clause _who is simple…_ + noun clauses _that she understands_ and _that the true person is…_. |
> | 7 | **Complex** | Conditional clause _If the world introduces…_ + main clause. |
> | 8 | **Simple** | One clause (imperative). |
> | 9 | **Compound** | Two imperative main clauses joined by _but_. |
> | 10 | **Complex** | Main clause _Act_ + subordinate clause _as though you knew_, which contains coordinated noun clauses _that the eyes… is upon you, and (that) you are living…_. (If _and you are living_ is read as a second main clause, the sentence is compound-complex.) |
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Clauses are identified by **finite verbs**. Non-finite forms (_to honour_, _endeavoring_, _being over-dressed_) don't create clauses. Imperatives (_Do not occupy…_) are clauses with an understood subject _you_.

## Simplified explanation

Count the finite verbs and look for words like **because, since, if, who, that** (complex) or **and, but** joining full clauses (compound).

body: State **three main challenges** in **oral presentation**, and in not more than three sentences suggest solutions to them.

**Coordination** joins ideas of **equal** importance with coordinating conjunctions (_and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so_) or correlatives (_both…and, not only…but also_), often by sharing a subject or object. **Subordination** makes one idea **dependent** on another using subordinators (_when, because, although, since, if, after, unless_) or relative pronouns (_who, which, that, whose_), showing time, cause, contrast or condition. _But_ coordinates the contrast; _because_ subordinates the reason.

## Simplified explanation

Use **and/but/yet** for equal ideas (coordination) or **when/because/although/who** to make one idea depend on another (subordination).
hint: Coordinators: and, but, or, yet, so. Subordinators: when, because, although, since, if, who, which, after.

Study carefully the passage below, and then write an **outline** or a **summary** of it.

> Obesity is a condition that results from excessive storage of fat in the body. It is now usually defined, using a formula known as the body mass index (BMI) … It has been estimated that roughly two thirds of American adults are overweight or obese …
>
> Obesity is a major public health concern because it predisposes the individual to many disorders, such as non-insulin-dependent diabetes, hypertension, stroke, and coronary disease. It has been associated with an increased incidence of certain cancers … Obese people are often ostracized, and discrimination against them, especially in hiring and promotion, is common.
>
> Obesity research has shown a number of underlying causes of the condition. The simple cause is ingestion of more calories than are required for energy … Inactivity and insufficient exercise can be contributing factors … Another cause is overeating which may result from unhealthy patterns of eating established by the family and cultural environment. This may perhaps be exacerbated by psychological distress, an emotional dependence on food, or the omnipresence of high-calorie foods.
>
> In some cases, obesity can come from an eating disorder. … Other studies have found a strong relationship between obesity in women and childhood sexual abuse.
>
> Some weight-loss experts see obesity as based upon genetics and physiology. … rat studies have shown that fat cells secrete a hormone that helps the rat's brain assess the amount of body fat present … resulting in the so-called set point—a weight that the body comes back to, even after resolute dieting. … It has been estimated that from 8 to 30 different genes may influence obesity.
>
> Radical treatments for weight loss have included wiring shut the jaw, operations that reduce the size of the stomach, and intestinal bypass operations … Drugs to treat the condition now include orlistat (Xenical) … The main possibility of treating obesity, however, remains diet and exercise, often coupled with emotional and behavioral support. The long-term weight-loss success of most attempts at dieting, however, is notoriously low. Groups such as Overeaters Anonymous … give support to people with weight problems and eating disorders.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (about 110 words):**
>
> Obesity, the excessive storage of body fat usually measured by the body mass index, affects many adults. It is a serious health concern because it predisposes people to diabetes, hypertension, stroke, heart disease and some cancers, and obese people also suffer social discrimination. It is caused mainly by consuming more calories than the body uses, aggravated by inactivity and overeating rooted in family and cultural habits or emotional distress. It may also stem from eating disorders, past abuse, or genetic and physiological factors that keep body weight at a fixed 'set point'. Treatments range from surgery and drugs to the main remedy of diet and exercise with emotional support, though long-term success is low.
>
> **Outline alternative:**
> 1. Definition and prevalence (BMI).
> 2. Health and social consequences.
> 3. Causes: excess calories, inactivity, overeating, emotional factors.
> 4. Eating disorders and abuse.
> 5. Genetic and physiological factors (set point).
> 6. Treatments: surgery, drugs, diet and exercise with support; low long-term success.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Omit illustrations (rat studies, specific cancers, Overeaters Anonymous, 8–30 genes, orlistat) and keep the generalisations (genetic factors, drugs, support groups).

## Simplified explanation

Say what obesity is, why it's **dangerous**, its **causes** (eating too much, inactivity, emotions, genes), and its **treatments** (mainly **diet and exercise**), in about 100 words.
hint: One point per paragraph; leave out statistics and examples.

**Restore all punctuation marks** (and correct capitalisation) in the following passage.

> Few weeks ago, the Kwame Nkrumah university of Science and technology was close down indefinitely following a violent demonstration by some students of the university. the demonstration by the students of the university against what they termed, tyrannical style of the university administration, turned unpleasant, leading to the massive destruction of public and private property. Media reports indicated that, the items destroyed included the following cars, furnitures, computers bill boards, flower pots et cetera. It will not be far fetched to conclude that, the remote cause of the riot is linked to the decision by the university to convert some of the halls into mixed halls. At a round-table discussion organized by a section of the public to deliberate on the matter at stake, the chairperson remarked, “lets ensure sanity prevails in our educational institutions therefore we call for an amicable resolution to the current challenges confronting the university.
answer:
> [!answer]
> A few weeks ago, the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology was closed down indefinitely following a violent demonstration by some students of the university. The demonstration by the students against what they termed the "tyrannical style" of the university administration turned unpleasant, leading to the massive destruction of public and private property. Media reports indicated that the items destroyed included the following: cars, furniture, computers, billboards, flower pots, et cetera. It will not be far-fetched to conclude that the remote cause of the riot is linked to the decision by the university to convert some of the halls into mixed halls. At a round-table discussion organised by a section of the public to deliberate on the matter at stake, the chairperson remarked, "Let's ensure sanity prevails in our educational institutions; therefore, we call for an amicable resolution to the current challenges confronting the university."
>
> _Key points:_ capitalise the institution's full name and the sentence opening _The_; **no comma** after _termed_ and _that_ (they introduce the object or noun clause); quotation marks for the coined phrase _"tyrannical style"_; a **colon** before the list, with commas between items (_furniture_ is uncountable, _billboards_ one word); the hyphen in _far-fetched_; _Let's_ (apostrophe); a **semicolon** before _therefore_; the closing quotation mark. (Grammar: _A few weeks ago_, _closed down_.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Over-punctuation is also an error: a comma should not separate a verb from its object or a reporting verb from a _that_-clause. A conjunctive adverb (_therefore, however_) joining two independent clauses requires a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

## Simplified explanation

Capitalise the university's name, use a **colon** before the list, **commas** between items, **'far-fetched'**, **'Let's'**, a **semicolon** before **'therefore'**, and close the **quotation**.
hint: Remove wrong commas too, not just add marks.

body:
Read the following passage and **correct any subject–verb agreement (concord) errors**. Do not copy the whole passage.

> For the past few years and particularly this year, there has been a number of grave concerns expressed by many Ghanaians regarding either safety conditions as well as security that prevails in the country. The migration of people in the major cities with limited chances of gainful jobs have also increased instances of many crimes. This set of unfortunate situations in Ghana lead to the undermining of development and progress of our country if drastic measures, as a matter of fact, is not taken to address them. As a country, we have to take a second look at our security agencies, particularly the Ghana Armed Forces which more often combats criminal activities. The government should resource the security agencies adequately to enable them to fight crime effectively. … it is the primary responsibility of the state to ensure the security of either the strong or the weak who lives in the country. We need to understand that security in conjunction with safety mechanisms promote peace and socio-economic development. It is incumbent on the public to report any litany of activities that poses a threat to national security. If we do not solve these problems, the majority is going to be blamed when the situation gets out of control.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _there **has** been a number of grave concerns_ → **there have been** (_a number of_ + plural).
> 2. _safety conditions as well as security that **prevails**_ → **prevail** (the antecedent is plural; also _either … as well as_ is faulty: use **both … and**).
> 3. _The migration of people … **have** also increased_ → **has** (head noun _migration_).
> 4. _This set of unfortunate situations … **lead**_ → **leads** (or _will lead_; head noun _set_).
> 5. _drastic measures … **is** not taken_ → **are not taken**.
> 6. _the Ghana Armed Forces which more often **combats**_ → **combat** (_Forces_ is plural).
> 7. _the strong or the weak who **lives**_ → **live** (_the strong/the weak_ = people, plural).
> 8. _security in conjunction with safety mechanisms **promote**_ → **promotes** (_in conjunction with_ is parenthetical; head noun _security_).
> 9. _any litany of activities that **poses**_ → **pose** (the antecedent _activities_ is plural).
>
> (_the majority is going to be blamed_ is acceptable: _majority_ as a single body.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Concord rules: the verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, ignoring intervening phrases; **compound subjects** with _and_ are plural; parenthetical additions (_together with, as well as, in conjunction with_) do not change the number; **relative pronouns** agree with their antecedents; in _there is/are_ sentences the verb agrees with the noun that follows; modal verbs and _to_-infinitives take the **base form**.

## Simplified explanation

Fix: **there have been**, **prevail**, **migration has**, **set leads**, **measures are**, **Armed Forces combat**, **the weak live**, **security promotes**, **activities pose**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject.

body:
Read the following passage carefully and write an **outline** of it.

> The sea turtles, especially the leatherbacks, are undoubtedly one of nature's most amazing creatures. They roam the warm seas of the world throughout their lives and come ashore only to lay eggs. Malaysia with its long sandy shorelines has been destined as one of their breeding grounds. Unfortunately, the number of leatherback turtles landing on the beaches has been declining over the years. … about 2000 leatherbacks arrived on Malaysian beaches in 1970. In 1989, only between 30 and 60 leatherbacks were found. … they may become an extinct species soon, that is, if no concerted effort is taken to check the decline now.
>
> The belief that the declining landings of turtles in Malaysia are the result of increasing landings in other parts of the world is a fallacy. … What has caused the species to dwindle at such rapid rate? There are many reasons but an obvious one is none other than man's greed. … turtles are killed for their meat. … Their shells have become coveted items for decorations and jewelry. Their eggs … are instead harvested and eaten. When deep sea fishing nets inadvertently trap the turtles, fishermen often kill the turtles instead of cutting their nets to release them. Pollution of the sea has also reduced the number of turtles. Many are choked to death by the plastic bags that they mistake for jellyfish. …
>
> Neither are they safe when the females come ashore to lay eggs. … The nesting places for these turtles have also been greatly reduced, as more and more beaches are taken over for tourism … The intrusion of tourists into these places makes it difficult for the turtles to lay their eggs. …
>
> Perhaps all is not lost yet. Sincere efforts are being taken to check the decline. In Malaysia … The indiscriminate collection of turtle eggs on the beaches is no more allowed. Turtle sanctuaries have been set up … The eggs collected by designated officials are sent to hatcheries in the sanctuaries. …
>
> In an effort to discourage the public from eating turtle eggs, a Turtle Enactment Act has been introduced to prohibit the sale of leatherback eggs. The WWF has also launched the 'Save the Turtle Campaign' to create an awareness among the public … Let us hope that it is not too late to save these fascinating creatures from becoming extinct.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Title: Saving the Leatherback Turtle**
>
> 1. **The problem: a sharp decline**
>    a. Leatherbacks come ashore only to lay eggs, e.g. in Malaysia.
>    b. Landings have fallen drastically, threatening extinction.
> 2. **Causes at sea**
>    a. Not migration elsewhere: the decline is worldwide.
>    b. Human greed: killing for meat and shells; harvesting of eggs.
>    c. Fishermen killing trapped turtles.
>    d. Sea pollution, especially plastic bags.
> 3. **Causes on land**
>    a. Vulnerability of females when nesting.
>    b. Loss of nesting beaches to tourism development.
>    c. Disturbance by tourists.
> 4. **Remedies**
>    a. A ban on the indiscriminate collection of eggs.
>    b. Sanctuaries and hatcheries.
>    c. A law prohibiting the sale of eggs.
>    d. Public awareness campaigns (WWF).
> 5. **Conclusion:** hope that the species can still be saved.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An **outline** shows the hierarchy of ideas: a **title**, **main points** (Roman or Arabic numerals) and **sub-points** (letters), written as **parallel phrases** (not full sentences), excluding examples and figures (2000 vs 30–60; Rantau Abang).

## Simplified explanation

Make headings: **the decline**, **causes at sea** (greed, nets, plastic), **causes on land** (tourism), **remedies** (sanctuaries, laws, campaigns) and a **conclusion**.
hint: Main headings with indented, parallel sub-points.

body:
Read the following passage carefully, and write an **outline or summary** of it (**90–120 words**).

> An occupation is all activity which an individual engages in. This activity is meaningful, purposeful and contributes to one's identity. … These occupations can include roles like being a parent, friend, spouse, tennis player, cook, or musician. We generally do not think about our daily occupations until we have trouble doing them. One way to avoid running into daily occupational troubles is by using occupational therapy. Occupational therapy (OT) incorporates your valued occupations into the rehabilitation process. …
>
> Occupational therapy is about health and rehabilitation. It is a client-centred health profession concerned with promoting health and well-being through occupation. The primary goal of occupational therapy is to enable people to participate in the activities of everyday life. It is practised in a wide range of public, private and voluntary sector settings such as the person's home environment, schools, workplaces, health centres, rehabilitation centres and hospitals. …
>
> Occupational therapists work with people of all ages who need specialized assistance to live independent, productive and satisfying lives due to physical, developmental, social or mental problems. They have a broad education in medical, social, behavioural, psychological, psychosocial and occupational sciences … The occupational therapist helps clients to perform all daily activities by improving muscle strength and endurance, balance and co-ordination, motor skills, modification of the environment, and modification of the task if necessary.
>
> People who benefit from the services of an OT include patients who suffer from orthopaedic conditions such as amputation, bone replacement and fracture; neurological conditions such as stroke, Parkinson's and spinal cord injuries; children with developmental and learning disabilities such as autism, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome …; psychiatric patients; and aged conditions such as arthritis and other degenerative conditions.
>
> Although the hospital or rehab facility is responsible for ensuring all issues relating to one's care and discharge are addressed, OTs provide comprehensive pre-admission and post-discharge home assessment to assist with the discharge planning. OTs also plan return-to-work programmes to enable clients to get back to the occupation they were engaged in even before the disability or illness.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Model summary (about 105 words):**
>
> An occupation is any meaningful, purposeful activity that shapes a person's identity, and people usually notice their occupations only when they struggle to perform them. Occupational therapy is a client-centred health profession that helps people regain the ability to carry out everyday activities as part of rehabilitation, in settings ranging from homes and schools to hospitals. Broadly trained occupational therapists help people of all ages with physical, developmental, social or mental problems to live independently by improving their strength, balance and motor skills and by adapting tasks and environments. Their clients include orthopaedic, neurological, developmental, psychiatric and elderly patients. Therapists also assist with discharge planning and return-to-work programmes.
>
> **Outline alternative:**
> 1. Meaning of occupation and the role of OT.
> 2. Nature and goal of OT; settings.
> 3. Occupational therapists: clients, training, methods.
> 4. Beneficiaries.
> 5. Discharge and return-to-work services.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Generalise long lists of examples (amputation, stroke, autism → orthopaedic, neurological, developmental conditions) and avoid copying sentences verbatim.

## Simplified explanation

Explain **what an occupation is**, **what OT does**, **who therapists help and how**, and their **discharge and return-to-work** roles, in about 100 words.
hint: Definition, nature, professionals, beneficiaries, other services.

> Diabetes comes about when the insulin levels in the body are low or the body cannot effectively utilize insulin. The lack of insulin in Type I could be due to attack by a virus … or … autoimmune disorders. Type II diabetes is mainly caused by genetic factors and lifestyle changes, including the use of steroids and conditions of stress. Excessive production of growth hormone … and tumours of the adrenal gland … all result in high sugar level in the blood.
>
> Complications in diabetes could be acute … or longer term … Acute complications include diabetic ketoacidosis … coma or even death. Other complications include damage to the eyes …, damage to the nerves …, and kidney damage. The disease also affects large blood vessels, which ultimately lead to stroke, heart attacks and atherosclerosis. … Erectile dysfunction in men is a common complication … and limb amputations may be necessary to save a patient's life.
>

>
> Diabetes is on the increase world-wide mainly because of unhealthy lifestyles. It is, therefore, very important that we all take the appropriate measures with the required willpower to prevent getting the disease. (Daily Graphic, 16 November 2011)

Read the following passage and **correct any subject–verb agreement (concord) errors**. Do not copy the whole passage.

> Christmas is an occasion that lends themselves to merrymaking. But traders are experiencing mixed feelings, as the long human and vehicular traffic in the central business districts of the commercial centres does not necessarily translates into sales. Commuters are also worried because at this time of the year, transport challenges rear its ugly heads. Christmas is one period when accident rates goes up because of the rush on the roads. Commercial drivers are eager to take advantage of the increased number of activities to maximize his sales, and in so doing they disregard road traffic regulations resulting in accidents. Statistics from the National Road Safety Commission (NRSC) indicates that more and more people are losing their lives to accidents on the road. The reason for this sad development are not far-fetched, as it is on record that about 90 percent of road accidents is caused by human error. The latest figures released by the NRSC shows that 26,621 lives were lost through road accidents from January 2000 to September 2013. This figure, although spanning a 13-year period, are quite frightening, making road accidents one of the major causes of death in the country.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _an occasion that lends **themselves**_ → **lends itself** (pronoun agreement with _occasion_).
> 2. _does not necessarily **translates**_ → **translate** (base form after _does_).
> 3. _transport challenges rear **its** ugly heads_ → **rear their ugly heads**.
> 4. _accident rates **goes** up_ → **go up**.
> 5. _Commercial drivers … to maximise **his** sales_ → **their** sales.
> 6. _Statistics … **indicates**_ → **indicate**.
> 7. _The reason … **are** not far-fetched_ → **The reason … is** (or _The reasons … are_).
> 8. _about 90 percent of road accidents **is** caused_ → **are caused** (percentage + plural noun).
> 9. _The latest figures … **shows**_ → **show**.
> 10. _This figure … **are** quite frightening_ → **is**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Concord rules: the verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, ignoring intervening phrases; **compound subjects** with _and_ are plural; parenthetical additions (_together with, as well as, in conjunction with_) do not change the number; **relative pronouns** agree with their antecedents; in _there is/are_ sentences the verb agrees with the noun that follows; modal verbs and _to_-infinitives take the **base form**.

## Simplified explanation

Fix: **lends itself**, **does not translate**, **rear their heads**, **rates go**, **their sales**, **statistics indicate**, **reason is**, **90 percent … are**, **figures show**, **figure is**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject.

Concerning present deterrents, Dr. Samuel Mensah, an expert in criminal law and psychology, write: “After a taste of prison, the criminal may become shrewder and more cautious, but he continues his exploitative way of life and commit crimes. Recidivism statistics indicates only whether he has been careless enough to be caught again.” In effect, then, prisons in Ghana often becomes finishing schools for criminals, inadvertently helping to hone their antisocial skills. What is more, many crimes that occur in the society goes unpunished, leading felons to conclude that crime does pay. The belief, even though convincing, make them bolder and more set in their ways.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _Studies … **shows**_ → **show**.
> 2. _the costs … **continues**_ → **continue**.
> 3. _does society **addresses**_ → **address** (base form after _does_).
> 4. _Dr Samuel Mensah, an expert …, **write**_ → **writes** (the appositive does not change the singular subject).
> 5. _he continues … and **commit** crimes_ → **commits** (parallel with _continues_).
> 6. _Recidivism statistics **indicates**_ → **indicate**.
> 7. _prisons in Ghana often **becomes**_ → **become**.
> 8. _many crimes that occur … **goes** unpunished_ → **go**.
> 9. _The belief … **make** them bolder_ → **makes**.

## Advanced explanation

Concord rules: the verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, ignoring intervening phrases; **compound subjects** with _and_ are plural; parenthetical additions (_together with, as well as, in conjunction with_) do not change the number; **relative pronouns** agree with their antecedents; in _there is/are_ sentences the verb agrees with the noun that follows; modal verbs and _to_-infinitives take the **base form**.

## Simplified explanation

Fix: **studies show**, **costs continue**, **does society address**, **Dr Mensah writes**, **commits**, **statistics indicate**, **prisons become**, **crimes go**, **belief makes**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject.

body:
Read the following passage carefully, and then **summarise it in 100 words**. Provide a **title**.

> The arming of policemen for certain jobs of law enforcement has become a controversial issue. In a country like the United States of America, where the carrying of guns is commonplace, shoot-outs with criminals have become accepted as part of the American culture. But in Great Britain and our own country, the public view armed policemen with suspicion and some hostility. Some people feel that only soldiers should carry guns, which they can handle efficiently.
>
> Experience has shown that armed policemen in many countries do not appear to have received sufficient training either physically or psychologically. Physically they seem unable to shoot accurately; they kill suspects, sometimes unarmed ones, instead of simply disabling them … Also, they are inclined to let their guns go off when, according to them, they didn't really intend to shoot. Psychologically, they seem unable to realize the extreme seriousness of shooting another human being, especially a suspect who may eventually turn out to be innocent … People cite tragic incidents bearing this out …
>
> But what of the other side? Is the disarming of the police really the answer? We have to remember that the nature of crime in the country, in fact, in the world, is changing. We must have more efficient ways of dealing with the new generation of violent criminals than the old unarmed police methods. Armed robbery has reached horrific proportions in many countries, and the armed robbers are often so desperate, sometimes under the influence of drugs …, that they will open fire even when they are met with no resistance. Any responsible government must be prepared to give its citizens adequate protection from such criminals by giving the police equal fire power. Also, we must not forget that these instruments of our protection, the police, are flesh and blood, with a life of their own to protect and with family responsibilities. The government is therefore obliged to equip them adequately for their dangerous job, so that a policeman in the course of duty will not feel he is being called upon to die prematurely.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Title: Should Policemen Be Armed?**
>
> **Model summary (about 100 words):**
>
> Arming the police is controversial. Although shoot-outs are accepted in America, the public in Britain and Ghana regard armed policemen with suspicion, and some believe only soldiers should carry guns. Many armed policemen are poorly trained physically and psychologically: they shoot inaccurately, kill suspects instead of disabling them, fire accidentally, and fail to appreciate the gravity of taking a possibly innocent life. However, disarming the police is no solution, because crime has become more violent and armed robbers, often drugged, shoot without provocation. Governments must therefore protect citizens and policemen alike by equipping the police with adequate weapons.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In argumentative passages, a summary must reflect the **structure of the argument** (the controversy, the case against, the case for, the writer's conclusion) without adding the summariser's opinion, and illustrative incidents (the bystander, the student) are omitted.

## Simplified explanation

Say arming police is **controversial**: they are **badly trained and kill innocent people**, but **violent armed robbers** mean the police **must be well armed** to protect citizens and themselves.
hint: Both sides: the case against, then the case for arming.

Read the following passage and write an **outline** of it.

> Armed robbery, one of the social evils in many developing countries, was relatively uncommon in the pre-independence era. … never has robbery with violence been experienced on such a wide scale as happens frequently these days.
>
> Prominent among the causes is the ubiquitous influence of crime stories and movies. Conscious of the fact that the youth care for excitement, script writers and film producers concentrate on such blood-curdling incidents as bank robbery, murder and arson. … The idle youth, naturally fascinated by what is shown, try to use them in real life situations.
>
> It is rather unfortunate that, in almost all modern societies, there are always groups of unemployable young people. They are unemployable because they have little or no education and lack skills. … They tend to blame society for their plight and retaliate by indulging in acts of crime and lawlessness. …
>
> The rich, on the other hand, who are mostly the target of armed robbers, provide another cause. Some flaunt their wealth, living ostentatiously, going about in flashy cars and hopping from one hotel to another in the company of teenagers on whom they lavish their wealth and leisure, to the anger and envy of the unemployed youth.
>
> Matters are compounded by the drug addiction among the youth. Their indulgence in drugs tends to deaden their consciences and make them prone to committing any kind of crime. … So a vicious cycle is set in motion …
>
> The break-down of traditional systems, resulting in loss of moral and spiritual values, has made wealth the only thing of value in the eyes of the youth. Many young people, therefore, try all means including armed robbery, to make money in order to enjoy the pleasures and comforts of modern life.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Title: Causes of Armed Robbery**
>
> 1. **Introduction:** armed robbery, once rare, is now widespread.
> 2. **Influence of crime stories and movies**
>    a. Producers' focus on violent, profitable content.
>    b. Imitation by idle youth.
> 3. **Unemployable youth**
>    a. Little education and no skills.
>    b. Unwillingness to do manual work.
>    c. Retaliation against society through crime.
> 4. **Ostentation of the rich**
>    a. Flaunting of wealth.
>    b. Anger and envy of the unemployed.
> 5. **Drug addiction**
>    a. Deadened consciences.
>    b. Robbery to fund drugs: a vicious cycle.
> 6. **Breakdown of traditional values**
>    a. Loss of moral and spiritual values.
>    b. Wealth as the only value.

## Advanced explanation

When a passage lists causes, the outline headings should be the **causes** themselves, with the explanations as sub-points.

List the causes: **crime movies**, **unemployable youth**, **show-off rich people**, **drugs** and **loss of traditional values**.

body:
Read the following passage and **correct any subject–verb agreement (concord) errors**. Do not copy the whole passage.

> Among the several factors that determines the choice of a national language are political neutrality. Bahasa in Indonesia and Tagalog in the Philippines are good examples. In Nigeria, there are simply no politically neutral language. In fact, the division into three major regions reflects the three language poles: Hausa, Yoruba and Ibo. In Ghana, neither Akan nor Ewe, the two most widely spoken languages, are politically neutral. The survival of Nigeria and Ghana as political entities will, therefore, be threatened if any one of these languages are promoted by the Government as the one national language.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. _factors that **determines**_ → **determine** (_that_ refers to the plural _factors_).
> 2. _Among the several factors … **are** political neutrality_ → **is** (in this **inverted** sentence the subject is _political neutrality_, singular).
> 3. _there **are** simply no politically neutral language_ → **there is** (the notional subject _language_ is singular).
> 4. _neither Akan nor Ewe … **are**_ → **is** (_neither … nor_ with two singular subjects takes a singular verb).
> 5. _if any one of these languages **are** promoted_ → **is** (head word _any one_).
>
> (_the division … reflects_ and _Bahasa … and Tagalog … are_ are correct.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Concord rules: the verb agrees with the **head noun** of the subject, ignoring intervening phrases; **compound subjects** with _and_ are plural; parenthetical additions (_together with, as well as, in conjunction with_) do not change the number; **relative pronouns** agree with their antecedents; in _there is/are_ sentences the verb agrees with the noun that follows; modal verbs and _to_-infinitives take the **base form**.

## Simplified explanation

Fix: **factors determine**, **is political neutrality**, **there is no … language**, **neither … nor … is**, **any one … is**.
hint: Find the head noun of each subject.

Rewrite the following passage, inserting the appropriate **punctuation** where necessary.

> In an early speech Lincoln said I am young and unknown to many of you I was born and have ever remained in the most humble walks of life I have no wealth no popular relations or friends to recommend me in this same speech is the characteristic little remark holding it as a sound maxim that it is better only sometimes to be right than at all times to be wrong the smile still lingers behind the words a characteristic statement of his was so soon as I discover my opinions to be erroneous I shall be ready to renounce them this was always his attitude towards the end of his life someone said to him why mr president you have changed your mind Lincoln answered yes I have and I dont think much of a man who isnt wiser today than he was yesterday
answer:
> [!answer]
> In an early speech, Lincoln said, "I am young and unknown to many of you. I was born and have ever remained in the most humble walks of life. I have no wealth, no popular relations or friends to recommend me." In this same speech is the characteristic little remark: "Holding it as a sound maxim that it is better only sometimes to be right than at all times to be wrong…" The smile still lingers behind the words. A characteristic statement of his was: "So soon as I discover my opinions to be erroneous, I shall be ready to renounce them." This was always his attitude. Towards the end of his life, someone said to him, "Why, Mr President, you have changed your mind!" Lincoln answered, "Yes, I have, and I don't think much of a man who isn't wiser today than he was yesterday."
>
> _Key points:_ quotation marks around each **direct quotation**; colons to introduce the formally announced remark and statement; commas after _In an early speech_ and _Towards the end of his life_; the **interjection** _Why_ and the **vocative** _Mr President_ set off by commas; **apostrophes** in _don't_ and _isn't_; sentence boundaries throughout.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Quotations introduced by a full independent clause (_A characteristic statement of his was_) may be preceded by a colon; interjections and terms of address are set off by commas; contractions require apostrophes.

## Simplified explanation

Put **quotation marks** around Lincoln's and the visitor's words, add **commas** after the opening phrases and around _Mr President_, **colons** before the quoted remarks, **apostrophes** in _don't_ and _isn't_, and split the sentences.
hint: Separate Lincoln's own words from the narrator's.

> Many years ago, we live on High Street in Accra. Before we move to this place, we stay in different parts of the city; Adabraka, Kaneshie and Achimota. But it is on High Street that we spend the most part of our childhood. While I attended the Government Girls' School situated at the other end of the street, my elder sister becomes a music tutor at Achimota School. She will visit us at the week-end whenever she feels bored at school. After I have completed my elementary education at the Government Girls' School, I went to do a teacher training course at Achimota School where I meet my sister again.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Many years ago, we **lived** on High Street in Accra. Before we **moved** to this place, we **had stayed** in different parts of the city: Adabraka, Kaneshie and Achimota. But it **was** on High Street that we **spent** the greater part of our childhood. While I **attended** the Government Girls' School situated at the other end of the street, my elder sister **became** a music tutor at Achimota School. She **would visit** us at the weekend whenever she **felt** bored at school. After I **had completed** my elementary education at the Government Girls' School, I **went** to do a teacher training course at Achimota School, where I **met** my sister again.

body:
Read the following passage carefully and write an **outline** of it.

> Many students treat the learning process as a passive one. Their view of it goes like this. You wait till the teacher comes in and starts teaching. … you listen to him, and take notes if he writes them and tells you to copy them. When the lesson is over, you close your book and leave it closed till the next lesson. Practically, at the end of the term or year, you learn by heart those comprehensive notes and pour them out during the examinations. Little or no learning, in fact, takes place.
>
> There are, however, a number of methods a student can employ to make his learning more effective. It is wise to get to know in advance what topics are planned for the week and eventually for the lesson. One can then do some reading on the topic beforehand; a quick skim will give an idea of the general direction of the writers' thoughts. Later, a more careful reading will give more details of information.
>
> During the lesson, the student must listen carefully and be ready to ask questions if he does not understand. If the teacher is going too fast, he can be asked to slow down. It is a good practice to try to pick out the important points as the lesson proceeds. These points may be written in a rough note book. … If the teacher gives notes to be copied, the students' own notes may be compared with these as a check. If the notes do not make sense, it is best to ask the teacher for clarification before the lesson ends.
>
> As soon as possible after the lesson, the notes should be re-read at intervals, so that the student can build up an overall picture of what has been taught so far. This will help him in understanding better where all the parts of the subject fit, and will make future lessons more comprehensible. In short, effective studying means repeated movement backwards and forwards over the area of study.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Title: Effective Learning**
>
> 1. **The passive approach to learning**
>    a. Waiting for the teacher and copying notes.
>    b. Neglecting notes until examinations.
>    c. Memorising notes, with little real learning.
> 2. **Before the lesson**
>    a. Finding out the topics in advance.
>    b. Skimming, then reading carefully.
> 3. **During the lesson**
>    a. Listening carefully and asking questions.
>    b. Asking the teacher to slow down.
>    c. Noting important points.
>    d. Checking own notes against the teacher's; seeking clarification.
> 4. **After the lesson**
>    a. Re-reading notes at intervals.
>    b. Building an overall picture of the subject.
> 5. **Conclusion:** effective study means repeated review of the area of study.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

When a passage describes a **process**, the outline can follow its **chronological stages**, contrasting the ineffective (passive) method with recommended active strategies.

## Simplified explanation

Headings: **passive learning (the problem)**, **before the lesson**, **during the lesson**, **after the lesson**, **conclusion: review repeatedly**.
